title: Accountants and auditors
rationale: Accounting workflows vary significantly across industries (banking, healthcare, manufacturing) and company sizes, requiring substantial customization around client-specific chart-of-accounts, regulatory frameworks, and internal controls. However, the addressable market is dominated by large enterprises and mid-market firms with substantial accounting operations, plus a concentrated segment of large CPA/accounting service providers (23% of employment) that serve many clients, making it feasible for a vendor to capture most buyer-side value through a few enterprise contracts.
repeatability_rationale: Accounting and auditing workflows are heavily dependent on each employer's proprietary accounting systems, chart of accounts, internal control frameworks, regulatory requirements, and industry-specific compliance standards. While data entry and routine reconciliation may be automatable across companies, the core analytical work—risk assessment, control testing, audit procedures, and financial statement analysis—must be substantially customized to each organization's specific accounting infrastructure, regulatory environment (government vs. public vs. internal audit), and business model, making agent transfer between employers require significant rebuilding.

title: Actuaries
rationale: Actuarial workflows vary significantly across insurance types (health, life, pension, property/casualty) and non-insurance sectors (enterprise risk, investments), with each requiring different regulatory frameworks, data sources, and modeling approaches specific to each company's product mix and risk profile. However, the buyer market is highly concentrated in large insurance companies and financial institutions (78% in finance/insurance) where a small number of major carriers and consulting firms dominate the addressable value for actuarial AI tools.
repeatability_rationale: Actuarial work is deeply bound to each employer's proprietary models, regulatory requirements, product lines, and legacy systems. While the mathematical frameworks are universal, the core tasks—designing insurance products, pricing policies, calculating reserves, and forecasting risk—require rebuilding the agent for different insurance lines (health vs. life vs. property), regulatory regimes (state vs. federal), company-specific underwriting rules, and custom databases that vary significantly across employers.

title: Air traffic controllers
rationale: Air traffic control workflows are highly standardized across all facilities, governed by FAA regulations, radar systems, and radio communication protocols that are uniform nationwide. The addressable market is concentrated among a small number of large airport operators (major hubs and regional facilities) that account for most air traffic volume and control complexity, with 90% of controllers employed by the federal government (FAA) itself.
repeatability_rationale: Air traffic control relies on highly standardized federal regulations, equipment, and procedures governed by the FAA, but the core workflow differs significantly based on facility type (tower, approach/departure, en route center), airspace complexity, airport geography, and real-time dynamic conditions that cannot be pre-scripted. An AI agent built to automate ATC tasks at one facility would require substantial rebuilding to operate safely and effectively at a different facility with different airspace, traffic patterns, runway configurations, and local procedures.

title: Atmospheric scientists, including meteorologists
rationale: Atmospheric scientists follow standardized scientific methodologies (data collection, computer modeling, forecasting) that are largely uniform across employers, making workflows highly repeatable. However, the addressable market is highly concentrated: 31% work in federal government (primarily NOAA/NWS), 16% in universities, and only 13% in dispersed professional services, meaning a dominant AI vendor could capture most value by serving NOAA and a small number of large research institutions and broadcasters.
repeatability_rationale: Atmospheric scientists' core work is fundamentally tied to scientific research methods, proprietary weather modeling systems, and domain-specific instruments (radar, satellites, weather balloons) that vary significantly between employers—from NOAA's operational forecasting infrastructure to broadcast networks' graphics systems to research institutions' custom models. An agent built for one employer's data collection, analysis, and forecasting workflow would require substantial rebuilding to handle another employer's different modeling approaches, data sources, and operational requirements.

title: Bill and account collectors
rationale: Bill collection workflows are highly standardized across industries—skip tracing, compliance with FDCPA/state laws, negotiation scripts, and payment plan recording follow similar patterns everywhere. However, the buyer market is fragmented: while third-party collection agencies (25%) and credit intermediation (19%) are significant, the work is distributed across healthcare, professional services, management companies, and many small creditors, with no dominant cohort of large buyers that a single vendor could capture with one configuration. The long tail of small and mid-market creditors managing their own collections prevents market concentration despite workflow repeatability.
repeatability_rationale: The core tasks of bill collectors—skip tracing, contacting debtors, negotiating repayment plans, recording interactions, and monitoring payments—follow a consistent workflow across employers despite industry variation. These tasks rely on standard databases, phone systems, CRM tools, and regulatory compliance (Fair Debt Collection Practices Act) that are largely configurable rather than fundamentally different; an agent built for one collection operation would transfer to another with configuration changes to account systems and creditor policies.

title: Bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks
rationale: Bookkeeping workflows are highly standardized across companies—transaction entry, reconciliation, report generation, and GL posting follow universal accounting principles and similar software (QuickBooks, NetSuite, etc.), making agent transfer straightforward with light configuration. However, the buyer market is fragmented across 1.6M jobs spread widely across small businesses, mid-market firms, and large enterprises with no dominant cohort; most value lies in the long tail of small employers and independent practitioners rather than a few large buyers, preventing any single vendor from capturing the market with one product.
repeatability_rationale: The core tasks—posting financial transactions, reconciling accounts, recording debits and credits, checking for accuracy, and producing standard reports—follow nearly identical patterns across all companies. While specific accounting software, chart of accounts structures, and reporting templates vary by employer, the underlying workflow logic (data entry, classification, reconciliation, verification) remains constant and requires only configuration rather than fundamental rebuilding of the agent's logic.

title: Budget analysts
rationale: Budget analysis workflows vary dramatically across government agencies, universities, and private companies due to idiosyncratic accounting systems, regulatory requirements, org structures, and funding models—an agent must be rebuilt for each buyer's context. However, the addressable buyer market is highly concentrated: 26% of jobs are in federal government, 15% in education, and 13-11% in state/local government, meaning a few large institutional buyers (federal agencies, state systems, large universities, major corporations) control most of the value and can sustain specialized vendor solutions with dedicated integrations to their finance systems and compliance frameworks.
repeatability_rationale: Budget analysts perform core repeatable tasks across employers: reviewing proposals for completeness and compliance, analyzing financial data, consolidating budgets, monitoring spending against approved budgets, and preparing reports explaining variances. These workflows follow consistent analytical and documentation patterns regardless of employer; differences are primarily configuration-based (which budget system, which reporting templates, which regulatory frameworks) rather than fundamental changes to the underlying task logic.

title: Cartographers and photogrammetrists
rationale: Cartography workflows are highly standardized around GIS/CAD tools and common data sources (satellite imagery, surveys, LiDAR), making agent logic portable across companies. However, the buyer market is concentrated in government (45% local + state + federal) and large engineering/consulting firms, where mapping budgets and volumes dominate—a vendor can capture substantial value by serving these institutional buyers with a shared platform, even though cartographers work across many smaller employers.
repeatability_rationale: The core tasks—collecting spatial data, analyzing geographic information, creating maps using GIS and CAD software, and integrating data from standard sources (surveys, LiDAR, satellite imagery)—follow consistent methodological patterns across employers regardless of industry. While output tailoring (map format, data sources, specific use cases) and software configurations vary by employer, the underlying workflow of data collection → analysis → visualization → map production remains fundamentally the same, making an agent built for one organization readily transferable with light configuration adjustments.

title: Claims adjusters, appraisers, examiners, and investigators
rationale: Claims adjustment workflows vary significantly across insurance types (property/casualty, health, life, auto) and individual insurers' underwriting standards, fraud detection rules, and settlement policies, requiring company-specific configuration. However, the addressable agent market is highly concentrated among a small set of large insurance carriers and government programs (35% in direct carriers, 15% in federal government, 7% in health carriers) that handle the vast majority of claim volume and spending, making it viable for a focused vendor to serve dominant buyers with shared infrastructure.
repeatability_rationale: Claims adjustment work is fundamentally shaped by each insurer's proprietary policy language, underwriting standards, claims management systems, and regulatory compliance requirements that vary significantly by state and insurance type. While the surface tasks (document review, damage assessment, settlement negotiation) appear similar across companies, the actual decision logic—what's covered, how much to reserve, fraud thresholds, and legal interpretations—is deeply embedded in each carrier's specific policies, systems, and risk appetite, requiring substantial rebuilding of the automation logic per employer rather than light configuration.

title: Compensation and benefits managers
rationale: Compensation and benefits management is deeply embedded in each organization's unique pay structures, regulatory environment, vendor relationships, and internal systems—what works at a tech company differs substantially from a bank or hospital. Additionally, while concentrated in larger employers, the 20,900 job holders are distributed across many industries and company sizes with no dominant buyer cohort, making it difficult for a single vendor to serve most of the market with one configuration.
repeatability_rationale: The core tasks—analyzing compensation data, monitoring market rates and regulations, designing pay structures, managing benefits vendors, ensuring compliance, and preparing budgets—follow consistent analytical and administrative patterns across organizations. While specific systems (payroll platforms, HRIS tools, vendor choices) and regulatory contexts vary, the underlying workflow logic remains transferable with configuration adjustments rather than fundamental redesign.

title: Compensation, benefits, and job analysis specialists
rationale: Compensation and benefits structures vary significantly across industries, company sizes, regulatory environments, and organizational philosophies, requiring substantial customization around each employer's specific pay scales, benefits packages, compliance obligations, and HR systems. The 107,000 workers are distributed across nearly every industry (18% in insurance, 13% in professional services, with significant long-tail employment) with no dominant buyer cohort, making the market fragmented across large enterprises, mid-market firms, and public sector organizations rather than concentrated in a few major players.
repeatability_rationale: The core tasks—analyzing compensation data, researching benefits trends, evaluating job descriptions, ensuring regulatory compliance, and preparing reports—follow consistent analytical and administrative patterns across employers. While specific compensation systems, benefits vendors, and regulatory requirements vary, these are configuration differences; the underlying workflow of data analysis, policy comparison, compliance checking, and recommendation documentation remains fundamentally similar and would transfer readily between organizations with minimal agent retraining.

title: Compliance officers
rationale: Compliance workflows are highly industry-specific and regulatory-environment-dependent, varying dramatically between finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and government sectors—making cross-company transfer of an agent difficult. The buyer market is highly fragmented across 418,000 compliance officer positions spread across diverse industries and employer sizes, with no dominant cohort of large enterprises accounting for most addressable value.
repeatability_rationale: Compliance officers' core work is fundamentally tied to industry-specific regulations, company-specific risk profiles, and proprietary compliance frameworks that vary dramatically across sectors (healthcare vs. finance vs. manufacturing vs. government). While some tasks like documentation and training delivery could transfer, the underlying logic of identifying compliance risks, developing policies, and conducting audits is deeply rooted in each employer's regulatory environment and bespoke processes, requiring substantial rebuilding of an agent's rule sets and assessment logic per employer.

title: Computer network architects
rationale: Network architecture is deeply idiosyncratic to each organization's existing infrastructure, security posture, scale, and technology stack—what works for a cloud-native startup differs fundamentally from a legacy bank or hospital system. The buyer market is also fragmented: while some large enterprises and telecoms need significant spend, network architecture work is distributed across virtually every mid-sized and large organization, with no dominant cohort that a single vendor can capture with one product.
repeatability_rationale: Computer network architects' core work is highly dependent on each organization's specific infrastructure, security requirements, existing systems, and proprietary architecture. While the general methodology (assessment, design, deployment, testing, documentation) is consistent, the actual technical tasks—selecting specific technologies, configuring particular network topologies, integrating with legacy systems, and implementing security postures—vary fundamentally based on each company's unique IT environment and business needs, making automation agents non-transferable without substantial rebuilding.

title: Computer support specialists
rationale: Computer support workflows vary dramatically across industries (healthcare EHR systems vs. telecom networks vs. financial institutions vs. education) and depend heavily on each organization's specific infrastructure, legacy systems, and IT architecture, making cross-company transfer difficult. The buyer market is highly fragmented, with support needs distributed across tens of thousands of small-to-medium employers, educational institutions, government agencies, and small businesses that cannot justify shared-infrastructure vendors—the top five employer sectors account for only ~55% of network support jobs and ~58% of user support jobs, leaving the majority spread across a long tail of organizations.
repeatability_rationale: Core support tasks—diagnosing problems, documenting issues, guiding users through troubleshooting steps, installing software/hardware, and escalating recurring problems—follow consistent patterns across companies. While the specific systems, tools, and products differ by employer, an agent trained on the fundamental diagnostic and communication workflows would transfer readily with light configuration for company-specific software stacks and ticket-management systems.

title: Cost estimators
rationale: Cost estimation workflows vary significantly across construction, manufacturing, and automotive sectors due to industry-specific methodologies, regulatory requirements, and proprietary systems (BIM, CAD, company databases); additionally, the 221,400 jobs are dispersed across thousands of small-to-medium specialty contractors, builders, and manufacturers with no dominant buyer cohort, making it difficult for a single vendor to capture most addressable value with shared infrastructure.
repeatability_rationale: Cost estimators perform core tasks—reading technical documents, identifying cost factors, calculating estimates, comparing against historical data, and documenting results—that follow consistent logical patterns across construction and manufacturing contexts. While the specific software (BIM, CAD, proprietary systems) and pricing databases differ by employer, the underlying workflow of data collection, analysis, and estimate generation remains fundamentally the same, making an agent built at one company readily transferable with configuration adjustments.

title: Credit counselors
rationale: Credit counseling workflows are highly standardized across organizations—financial assessment, debt analysis, budget planning, and client education follow similar processes regardless of employer. However, the buyer market is fragmented: the largest single employer category (universities) accounts for only 36% of jobs, with the remaining positions spread across hospitals, credit unions, nonprofits, and small financial institutions, meaning no single vendor can capture dominant value through one configuration.
repeatability_rationale: Credit counselors perform core repeatable tasks—financial assessment, debt analysis, budget planning, client education, and documentation—that follow consistent logical patterns across employers. While specific financial tools, creditor databases, and institutional policies vary by employer, these differences are configuration-level rather than fundamental workflow changes, making an agent trained at one organization readily transferable to another with minimal rebuilding.

title: Customer service representatives
rationale: Customer service workflows are standardized across most industries—listening to concerns, processing orders, handling complaints, and recording interactions follow similar patterns regardless of employer. However, the addressable AI agent market is highly concentrated among large enterprises (retail chains, insurance carriers, telecoms, banks) that handle massive ticket volumes and can justify significant infrastructure investment; most value derives from a relatively small set of large organizations rather than the long tail of small businesses where customer service also exists.
repeatability_rationale: The core automatable tasks—listening to customer inquiries, retrieving product/service information, processing orders and payments, handling returns, and documenting interactions—follow consistent patterns across companies and industries. While specific products, systems, and regulatory requirements vary by employer (retail vs. insurance vs. utilities), the underlying workflow logic remains the same; an agent trained on these foundational tasks would transfer across employers with primarily configuration changes (different CRM systems, product databases, billing platforms) rather than fundamental process redesign.

title: Data scientists
rationale: Data science workflows vary dramatically across industries and companies due to differences in data infrastructure, domain-specific problems, regulatory requirements, and internal analytics maturity; an agent must be rebuilt around each organization's data stack, business context, and analytical priorities. While data science spans many sectors (tech, insurance, consulting, finance, research), the addressable value is distributed across a large, heterogeneous buyer base with no dominant cohort—most organizations need data scientists but few have the scale to support a standardized vendor solution like the largest enterprises in customer service or legal review.
repeatability_rationale: Data scientists' core tasks—data collection, cleaning, exploratory analysis, algorithm development, validation, and visualization—follow consistent methodological patterns across companies regardless of industry. While the specific datasets, business domains, and tools differ, the underlying workflow and analytical logic remain fundamentally similar, making an agent built for these tasks readily transferable with configuration changes (different data sources, visualization platforms, or domain context) rather than requiring structural rebuilding.

title: Database administrators and architects
rationale: Database administration and architecture workflows vary significantly across organizations due to differing database technologies, cloud strategies, data governance frameworks, and compliance requirements (finance vs. healthcare vs. retail). However, the buyer market is concentrated: the largest employers are in computer systems design, finance/insurance, and large enterprises that account for the majority of addressable value, making this attractive for specialized vendors serving the high-spend segment.
repeatability_rationale: Database administration and architecture are heavily dependent on proprietary systems, vendor-specific tools (Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, cloud platforms like AWS/Azure), and organization-specific data schemas, security policies, and infrastructure. An agent built for one company's database environment would require substantial rebuilding to handle different database management systems, security protocols, backup strategies, and application-specific requirements at another company.

title: Epidemiologists
rationale: Epidemiological workflows vary significantly by specialization (infectious disease, chronic disease, environmental health, etc.), employer type (CDC/NIH, state/local health departments, hospitals, pharma), and regulatory/institutional context, requiring substantial customization per organization. However, the buyer market is highly concentrated: 34% of jobs are in state government and 22% in local government, with major federal agencies (CDC, NIH) and large hospital systems accounting for most addressable AI value, making this a natural fit for a few specialized vendors to serve dominant public health institutions.
repeatability_rationale: Epidemiologists' core work is heavily dependent on each employer's specific disease focus, regulatory environment, data systems, and research infrastructure—whether working for CDC on federal surveillance, a state health department on outbreak response, a hospital on infection control, or a pharmaceutical company on drug trials. The underlying investigative logic and statistical methods may be similar, but the actual tasks (which diseases to track, which data systems to query, which populations to study, which reporting requirements to meet) differ fundamentally by organization, making substantial workflow reconfiguration necessary for each employer.

title: Financial analysts
rationale: Financial analysts' workflows vary significantly across institutions due to different investment mandates, risk frameworks, compliance regimes, and proprietary data systems (hedge funds vs. banks vs. insurance companies operate under fundamentally different constraints and strategies). However, the buyer market is highly concentrated: the addressable value is dominated by large asset managers, banks, insurance companies, and hedge funds that collectively employ most of the 429,000 analysts and control the majority of assets under management, making it possible for a single vendor to capture substantial market share by serving this institutional cohort with configurable rather than fully bespoke solutions.
repeatability_rationale: Financial analysts' core work is deeply bound to proprietary trading systems, risk models, portfolio management platforms, and client-specific investment mandates that vary fundamentally between securities firms, hedge funds, banks, and insurance companies. An agent built for buy-side portfolio optimization would require substantial rebuilding for sell-side equity research or ratings analysis, and again for risk assessment in a credit institution, because the underlying analytical logic, data inputs, regulatory constraints, and decision criteria are fundamentally different across these contexts.

title: Financial clerks
rationale: Financial clerks encompass highly specialized subtypes (billing, payroll, brokerage, loan processing, insurance claims) with vastly different workflows, systems, and regulatory requirements across industries—an agent built for insurance claims processing will not transfer to brokerage or payroll work. The 1.2M workers are distributed across insurance (20%), healthcare (18%), credit intermediation (16%), and many smaller sectors with no dominant buyer cohort; most employers are mid-market and smaller firms where the addressable value per deployment is low, making it economically infeasible for a vendor to capture most of the market with a single product.
repeatability_rationale: Financial clerks perform core tasks that follow consistent patterns across employers: data entry, record-keeping, calculations, transaction processing, and customer account management. While the specific systems (insurance platforms, loan management software, payroll systems) differ by employer, the underlying workflows—verify information, calculate amounts, update records, process transactions—remain fundamentally the same and would require only configuration changes, not algorithmic redesign.

title: Financial examiners
rationale: Financial examiners' workflows are highly regulated and institution-specific, varying by regulatory framework (federal vs. state oversight), institution type (banks, credit unions, securities firms), and internal compliance systems—requiring deep customization per employer. However, the buyer market is concentrated: 42% of jobs are in credit intermediation, federal/state regulators are major employers, and a small cohort of large financial institutions and regulators account for most of the compliance spend and examination volume, making this attractive for a vendor targeting systemically important banks and regulatory agencies.
repeatability_rationale: Financial examiners work within heavily regulated, institution-specific frameworks where examination procedures, compliance requirements, and risk assessment methodologies vary significantly by regulatory agency (federal vs. state), institution type (banks, credit unions, securities firms), and regulatory posture. An agent built for one employer's examination process would require substantial rebuilding to handle different regulatory regimes, proprietary banking systems, loan portfolio structures, and compliance documentation standards across other institutions.

title: Financial managers
rationale: Financial management workflows vary substantially across industries (banking, healthcare, government, manufacturing) due to sector-specific regulations, accounting standards, and capital structures, requiring agents to be rebuilt for each industry context. However, the buyer market is concentrated in large financial institutions, Fortune 500 companies, and major government agencies that account for most of the addressable value and have the resources to deploy sophisticated financial AI systems.
repeatability_rationale: Financial managers' core work is deeply bound to each organization's proprietary financial systems, accounting structures, regulatory requirements, and strategic priorities. While data analysis and reporting are common, the specific calculations, compliance frameworks (government vs. healthcare vs. banking), investment strategies, and decision-making processes differ fundamentally across industries and individual companies, requiring substantial rebuilding of an agent per employer rather than light configuration.

title: General office clerks
rationale: General office clerk duties vary significantly by industry context (colleges process applications, hospitals manage medical records, construction handles project documentation), requiring customization to each employer's specific systems, workflows, and organizational structure. The 2.6M workers are distributed across highly fragmented buyers—education (13%), healthcare (11%), construction (10%), government (10%), and dozens of other sectors—with no dominant cohort of large employers that would allow a single vendor to capture most addressable value with a shared platform.
repeatability_rationale: Core tasks like answering phones, typing/formatting documents, filing records, scheduling appointments, data entry, and mail sorting follow standardized patterns across all employers—differences are primarily configuration-based (which phone system, which filing structure, which software platform). While specific content varies by industry (hospital medical records vs. university applications), the underlying workflow logic and automation potential remain consistent.

title: Geographers
rationale: Geographic research workflows vary significantly by domain (physical vs. human geography), client needs (urban planning vs. environmental assessment vs. resource management), and regulatory/institutional context, requiring customized GIS integrations and data sources for each organization. However, 68% of geographers work in federal government, creating a highly concentrated buyer market where a single vendor could serve most of the addressable value through tailored solutions for federal agencies and large state/local governments managing infrastructure and environmental planning projects.
repeatability_rationale: Geographic research is highly context-dependent, requiring domain expertise in specific regional systems, environmental conditions, regulatory frameworks, and stakeholder relationships that differ fundamentally across projects and employers. While GIS software and data visualization tools are standardized, the underlying research methodology, data sources, analytical approach, and interpretation of geographic phenomena are tailored to each study's unique geographic, political, and institutional context, making substantial rebuilding necessary for each new employer or research domain.

title: Health information technologists and medical registrars
rationale: Workflow repeatability is low because health information technologists work across diverse healthcare settings (hospitals, physician offices, research institutions) with highly variable EHR systems, data governance policies, and clinical registries that differ substantially by organization and specialty. Concentration is fragmented because while hospitals dominate employment at 46%, the remaining 54% is spread across physician offices, management companies, and technical services firms—and even within hospitals, the work is deeply embedded in institution-specific systems, compliance frameworks, and clinical workflows that resist standardization across buyers.
repeatability_rationale: Health information technologists and medical registrars work with organization-specific healthcare systems, clinical databases, and disease registries that vary significantly in architecture, data structure, and regulatory requirements across hospitals, physician offices, and research institutions. While some tasks like data validation and report generation follow general patterns, the core work of system implementation, clinical data abstraction, and registry maintenance is deeply dependent on each employer's proprietary systems, coding standards, and institutional workflows, requiring substantial rebuilding per organization.

title: Human resources specialists
rationale: HR specialist workflows vary significantly across companies due to different organizational structures, compensation systems, benefits packages, and regulatory requirements; moreover, while 944k workers hold this role, the buyer market is highly fragmented across employers of all sizes (from small businesses to large enterprises), with no dominant cohort where a single vendor can capture most addressable value.
repeatability_rationale: Core HR specialist tasks like applicant screening, reference checking, benefits administration, policy compliance documentation, and employee record-keeping follow standardized workflows across organizations. While specific HR systems, benefits packages, and compliance regulations vary by employer, these differences are configuration-level; the underlying process logic for recruiting, onboarding, records management, and policy communication remains consistent and readily transferable.

title: Information clerks
rationale: Information clerks perform highly heterogeneous work across different subtypes (court clerks, eligibility interviewers, hotel desk clerks, file clerks, order clerks, etc.) with fundamentally different workflows, regulatory contexts, and systems (court dockets, government benefit systems, hotel management software, filing protocols), making agent reuse across companies minimal. The 1.3 million-person workforce is distributed across many small employers (traveler accommodation at 19%, healthcare at 11%, state government at 9%) with no dominant buyer cohort—most organizations that employ information clerks are fragmented across small and mid-sized companies, hotels, and government agencies, so no single vendor can capture most addressable value with one configuration.
repeatability_rationale: Information clerks perform core automatable tasks—data entry, record maintenance, answering routine inquiries, processing applications, and document filing—that follow consistent patterns across employers despite industry variation. While employer-specific systems (CRMs, booking platforms, government databases) differ, the underlying workflow logic (collect data, validate against criteria, file/respond, track status) remains substantially the same, making an agent built at one company readily transferable with configuration adjustments.

title: Information security analysts
rationale: Information security workflows are highly idiosyncratic, shaped by each organization's unique infrastructure, threat model, compliance requirements (finance vs. healthcare vs. tech), and existing security stack—making agent transfer between companies difficult. However, the buyer market is concentrated: large enterprises in finance, tech, and managed services (which collectively employ most analysts and represent the majority of security spend) have the resources and need for sophisticated security agents, while small businesses typically cannot afford or justify dedicated security infrastructure for agent deployment.
repeatability_rationale: Information security analysts' core work is deeply bound to each organization's proprietary systems, network architecture, security tools, regulatory requirements, and threat landscape; while some tasks like vulnerability scanning or report generation follow repeatable patterns, the security standards, disaster recovery procedures, threat detection logic, and remediation strategies must be substantially rebuilt per employer due to fundamental differences in infrastructure, industry compliance needs, and organizational risk profiles.

title: Insurance underwriters
rationale: Insurance underwriting workflows vary significantly by insurance type (health, life, property & casualty), regulatory environment, and company-specific risk models and approval criteria, making agent transfer difficult. However, the addressable market is concentrated in a small number of large direct insurance carriers and health insurers that dominate employment and underwriting volume, making it economically viable for a specialized vendor to build a deep product for this buyer cohort despite workflow heterogeneity.
repeatability_rationale: Insurance underwriting relies on proprietary underwriting software systems, company-specific risk assessment criteria, and regulatory frameworks that vary significantly by insurer, insurance type (health, life, property/casualty), and state regulations. While the surface workflow appears standardized, the core decision-making logic—risk evaluation rules, premium calculation models, and approval thresholds—is deeply embedded in each company's underwriting guidelines and systems, requiring substantial reconfiguration rather than light configuration to transfer an agent across employers.

title: Lawyers
rationale: Legal work workflows vary dramatically across practice areas (corporate, litigation, tax, IP, family law) and across different organizational contexts (BigLaw firms, in-house counsel, government, solo practice), each with distinct procedural rules, document templates, and client management systems. However, the addressable market for AI agents is highly concentrated in large law firms and major corporate legal departments where volume and budget enable significant AI investment.
repeatability_rationale: Legal work is fundamentally bound to jurisdiction-specific statutes, case law, regulatory frameworks, and procedural rules that vary significantly across states and practice areas, requiring substantial rebuilding of legal reasoning and document generation logic for each new jurisdiction or legal specialty rather than simple configuration changes.

title: Librarians and library media specialists
rationale: Library workflows vary significantly by institution type (public, academic, school, special/corporate) with different systems, patron bases, collection management practices, and organizational structures, requiring substantial customization per employer. The buyer market is highly fragmented across 142,100+ jobs distributed among local governments (32%), schools (31%), colleges (18%), and corporate/special libraries (5%), with no dominant cohort where a single vendor could capture most addressable value.
repeatability_rationale: Core librarian tasks—cataloging materials, managing databases, conducting reference research, evaluating information sources, organizing collections, and planning patron programs—follow standardized library science principles and methods that transfer across institutions. While specific systems (ILS software, databases, organizational structures) differ by employer, the underlying workflow logic remains consistent and requires only configuration rather than fundamental redesign of agent capabilities.

title: Loan officers
rationale: Loan underwriting workflows vary significantly across lenders due to different risk appetites, regulatory environments (mortgage vs. commercial vs. consumer), product portfolios, and internal approval hierarchies—an agent built for one bank's process requires substantial reconfiguration for another. However, the buyer market is highly concentrated: the largest employers (commercial banks, credit unions, mortgage companies) control most lending volume, and a vendor can capture significant value by selling to a small cohort of large financial institutions rather than serving thousands of small lenders.
repeatability_rationale: Loan officers' core work is deeply bound to each employer's proprietary underwriting systems, risk assessment frameworks, regulatory compliance requirements, and credit policies, which vary significantly across banks, mortgage companies, and credit unions. While data collection and verification tasks appear standardized, the actual underwriting logic, decision-making criteria, loan product offerings, and regulatory obligations differ fundamentally from one financial institution to another, requiring substantial rebuilding of an agent per employer rather than simple configuration.

title: Logisticians
rationale: Logisticians' workflows vary dramatically by industry (manufacturing vs. federal government vs. wholesale trade), product type, and company-specific supply chain architecture, ERP systems, and procurement processes—requiring substantial customization per employer. The buyer market is also highly fragmented, with 241,000 logisticians spread across manufacturing (23%), government (16%), professional services (15%), wholesale (11%), and many other sectors, so no single vendor can serve most of the addressable value with one configuration.
repeatability_rationale: Logisticians' core work is deeply embedded in each company's proprietary supply chain systems, procurement platforms, inventory management software, and business-specific logistics workflows. While general tasks like data analysis and cost optimization follow similar logic, the actual execution depends heavily on custom ERPs, specialized logistics software (which vary by industry and company), regulatory requirements specific to the sector (manufacturing vs. defense vs. e-commerce), and bespoke supplier/customer relationships that cannot transfer between employers without substantial rebuilding.

title: Market research analysts
rationale: Market research workflows are fundamentally similar across companies: define research questions, design surveys/studies, collect and analyze data with standard statistical tools, and present findings—these methods are largely industry-agnostic and transferable. However, the buyer market is highly fragmented; while 941,700 analysts are spread across all industries with no dominant employer cohort (largest is only 10% in consulting services), and small-to-mid-market companies each need their own research conducted, making it difficult for any single vendor to achieve scale with a shared product.
repeatability_rationale: Market research analysts perform standardized core tasks—data collection via surveys/interviews, statistical analysis, trend forecasting, and report generation with visualizations—that follow consistent methodologies across industries and companies. While specific clients, datasets, and presentation templates vary by employer, the underlying analytical workflow and tools (statistical software, survey design, data visualization) remain fundamentally the same, requiring only configuration changes rather than substantial process rebuilds.

title: Material recording clerks
rationale: Material recording workflows vary significantly across manufacturing, retail, wholesale, and transportation sectors—each with distinct inventory systems, production schedules, regulatory requirements, and operational structures that require custom integration. The market is also highly fragmented across 1.3 million workers distributed broadly across small to medium manufacturers, retailers, and warehouses rather than concentrated in a few dominant buyers, making it difficult for a single vendor to capture substantial value.
repeatability_rationale: Material recording clerks perform core tasks—inventory tracking, barcode scanning, record-keeping, shipping/receiving documentation, and quality inspections—that follow standardized patterns across companies. While specific inventory management systems, warehouse layouts, and product types vary by employer, the underlying workflow logic (scan items, update records, verify accuracy, prepare shipping documents) remains consistent and would transfer with configuration to different systems and templates.

title: Mathematicians and statisticians
rationale: Mathematicians and statisticians apply domain-specific analytical methods to highly varied problems across distinct sectors (pharma, aerospace, finance, government, R&D), requiring deep retraining for each industry's data structures, regulatory constraints, and business logic. However, the buyer market is concentrated in large organizations with substantial data infrastructure and budgets—federal government (17% of statisticians), major R&D firms, healthcare systems, and tech companies—where a vendor can capture significant value by building industry-specific solutions for each large buyer cohort rather than serving a long tail of small employers.
repeatability_rationale: The core tasks—designing experiments, collecting and analyzing data, identifying trends, conducting statistical tests, and presenting findings—follow consistent methodological patterns across industries and employers. An AI agent trained on data analysis workflows (survey design, statistical modeling, hypothesis testing, visualization) would transfer readily between companies with only configuration changes to domain-specific data formats, software tools, and output templates rather than fundamental rewiring of the analytical logic.

title: Medical dosimetrists
rationale: Medical dosimetry workflows vary significantly across institutions due to different radiation oncology equipment, treatment planning software systems, institutional protocols, and cancer case mixes, requiring substantial customization per hospital or center. However, the buyer market is highly concentrated among large hospital systems and cancer centers that perform high-volume radiation therapy, where a single vendor can capture substantial addressable value with a specialized solution.
repeatability_rationale: Medical dosimetry involves highly specialized physics-based calculations, clinical decision-making, and regulatory compliance that are bound to each institution's radiation oncology protocols, equipment specifications, treatment planning systems, and physician-defined dosage parameters. While the general workflow (review scans, calculate dose, design plan) is consistent, the underlying task logic—including dose algorithms, equipment-specific calibrations, institutional clinical guidelines, and treatment plan optimization—differs fundamentally between hospitals and clinics, requiring substantial rebuilding of an AI agent per employer.

title: Medical records specialists
rationale: Medical records workflows—data entry, coding, verification, and EHR management—are highly standardized across healthcare settings, relying on universal classification systems (ICD, CPT) and common EHR platforms, enabling an agent built for one organization to transfer to others with light configuration. The addressable market is dominated by large hospitals and health systems (28% of jobs) and big physician office networks, where transaction volume and reimbursement stakes justify AI investment, while the fragmented tail of small practices has lower individual spend.
repeatability_rationale: Medical records specialists perform standardized core tasks—reviewing records for completeness, assigning clinical codes using universal classification systems (ICD, CPT), maintaining EHR data, and ensuring confidentiality—that follow the same workflow logic across hospitals, physician offices, and healthcare facilities. While EHR systems and specific templates vary by employer, the underlying task patterns (data entry, code assignment, record verification, access control) are configuration differences rather than fundamental workflow changes, making an agent highly transferable with light setup adjustments.

title: Medical transcriptionists
rationale: Medical transcription workflows are highly standardized across healthcare settings—listen to dictation, convert to text, edit for accuracy, and enter into EHR systems—with minimal variation in the core process. However, the buyer market is fragmented: while hospitals and large health systems exist, the majority of transcriptionists work in small physician offices (36%) and independent transcription service companies (36%), with no dominant cohort of buyers that a single vendor could serve with shared infrastructure.
repeatability_rationale: Medical transcription involves core repeatable tasks—listening to dictation, converting speech to text, editing for accuracy, and entering records into EHR systems—that follow the same workflow across different healthcare settings. While EHR systems and medical templates may differ by employer, the fundamental transcription logic, error-checking process, and documentation standards remain consistent; configuration of specific system interfaces would be sufficient for agent transfer across most employers.

title: Network and computer systems administrators
rationale: Network administration workflows vary significantly across organizations due to idiosyncratic infrastructure, legacy systems, security policies, and vendor choices—an agent built for one company's stack (Azure/AWS/on-prem mix, specific monitoring tools, escalation rules) requires substantial reconfiguration elsewhere. The buyer market is also fragmented: while some large enterprises have significant IT infrastructure spend, the 331,500 jobs are distributed across every sector (education, finance, manufacturing, healthcare, government) with no dominant cohort—most organizations need their own admins rather than buying a shared vendor solution.
repeatability_rationale: Network and Computer Systems Administrators work with highly proprietary and company-specific infrastructure—each organization's network topology, security policies, hardware configurations, cloud platforms, and legacy systems are fundamentally different. An agent built to automate core tasks (configuration management, security hardening, performance monitoring, user provisioning) would require substantial rebuilding for each employer's unique architecture, compliance requirements, and technology stack, making transfer across companies infeasible without major reimplementation.

title: Operations research analysts
rationale: Operations research workflows are highly problem-specific and depend on each organization's unique business models, data infrastructure, supply chains, and decision-making structures—an airline scheduling model differs fundamentally from financial portfolio optimization or healthcare resource allocation. However, the buyer market is concentrated: 25% of employment is in finance/insurance and 22% in professional services, with the largest addressable value concentrated in large enterprises and government agencies (Federal government alone accounts for 6% of jobs) that have the scale and complexity to justify custom OR analysis and agent infrastructure.
repeatability_rationale: Operations research analysts' core work is deeply tied to each employer's specific business problems, proprietary data systems, domain expertise requirements, and organizational constraints. While the general methodological toolkit (statistical analysis, modeling, optimization) transfers across companies, the actual problem formulation, data architecture, stakeholder dynamics, and solution constraints vary fundamentally—requiring substantial recalibration of the analytical approach, not merely configuration of tools.

title: Paralegals and legal assistants
rationale: Paralegal work varies significantly across practice areas (litigation, bankruptcy, IP, corporate) and firm sizes, requiring deep familiarity with each firm's case management systems, document protocols, and attorney workflows. However, the addressable agent market is highly concentrated in large law firms and corporate legal departments that handle high-volume document work and can justify custom AI infrastructure investment.
repeatability_rationale: Paralegals' core work is deeply bound to each firm's proprietary case management systems, document management protocols, specific practice areas (bankruptcy, IP, litigation, family law), and bespoke legal procedures that vary significantly by jurisdiction and firm size. While tasks like research and drafting are nominally similar, the underlying workflows—from how documents are classified and stored to how discovery is managed to how trial logistics are coordinated—differ fundamentally enough that an agent built for one firm would require substantial rebuilding to handle another's specific legal processes, case structures, and compliance requirements.

title: Property appraisers and assessors
rationale: Property appraisal workflows vary significantly by geography, property type (residential vs. commercial), local tax assessment procedures, and state licensing requirements, requiring substantial customization per jurisdiction. The market is highly fragmented across 37% local government assessors in different municipalities, 21% self-employed appraisers, and distributed real estate/finance firms, with no dominant buyer cohort that a single vendor could serve at scale with a standardized product.
repeatability_rationale: Property appraisal and assessment work is heavily dependent on local jurisdiction regulations, tax codes, comparable property databases, and state-specific licensing requirements that vary significantly across companies and localities. Core task logic—determining property values, defending assessments, maintaining jurisdiction-specific property records—is fundamentally tied to each employer's regulatory environment and proprietary data systems, requiring substantial rebuilding of an agent per employer rather than simple configuration.

title: Public safety telecommunicators
rationale: Dispatch workflows vary significantly by jurisdiction due to differences in local geography, agency protocols, equipment systems (CAD platforms), multi-agency coordination rules, and state/municipal regulatory requirements—making cross-jurisdiction agent transfer difficult. The 105,200 jobs are spread across 78% local government plus state and private ambulance services with no dominant buyer cohort; thousands of independent municipalities and PSAPs would each need customized solutions, preventing any single vendor from capturing most market value with a standardized product.
repeatability_rationale: Public safety telecommunicators rely on agency-specific computer-aided dispatch (CAD) systems, local geography knowledge, jurisdiction-specific protocols and procedures, and distinct legal/regulatory frameworks that vary significantly by state and locality. An AI agent built for one 911 center's workflow would require substantial rebuilding to handle another agency's unique systems, dispatch procedures, local law enforcement protocols, and emergency response structures.

title: Purchasing managers, buyers, and purchasing agents
rationale: Purchasing workflows vary dramatically across industries (manufacturing vs. retail vs. government), company size, regulatory environments, and supplier ecosystems—requiring deep integration with each organization's ERP, contract management, and vendor systems. The buyer base is highly fragmented across manufacturing, wholesale, government, retail, and professional services with no dominant cohort; while large enterprises need procurement automation, the addressable value is spread across thousands of independent companies with idiosyncratic procurement policies and supplier networks.
repeatability_rationale: Purchasing workflows are heavily bound to each company's proprietary procurement systems, supplier networks, contract templates, approval hierarchies, and industry-specific regulations (manufacturing vs. retail vs. government have fundamentally different compliance and sourcing logic). While individual tasks like price analysis or contract negotiation follow similar patterns, the core work logic—which suppliers to evaluate, what compliance rules apply, which procurement systems to use, and how to structure deals—differs substantially enough that an agent would require significant rebuilding per employer rather than light configuration.

title: Receptionists
rationale: Receptionist workflows are highly standardized across employers—greeting visitors, answering phones, scheduling appointments, and data entry follow nearly identical patterns whether at a small office or large corporation, making agents transferable with minimal configuration. However, the buyer market is fragmented: receptionists are distributed across ~1 million employers spanning healthcare, professional services, nonprofits, and small businesses with no dominant buyer cohort, so no single vendor can capture most addressable value with one product.
repeatability_rationale: Core receptionist tasks—answering phones, scheduling appointments, greeting visitors, entering data, and managing correspondence—follow nearly identical patterns across organizations. While specific systems (phone systems, calendars, databases) and industry contexts vary, the underlying workflow logic is consistent and largely configuration-driven rather than fundamentally different from employer to employer.

title: Secretaries and administrative assistants
rationale: Administrative workflows are highly idiosyncratic across companies—varying by industry (healthcare vs. legal vs. general), organizational structure, executive preferences, and embedded systems (email, calendar, filing protocols, vendor relationships)—requiring substantial customization per employer. The 3.5 million workers are distributed across nearly every industry and organization size, with no dominant buyer cohort; value is spread across millions of small, medium, and large employers, making it impossible for a single vendor to capture most of the market with one product configuration.
repeatability_rationale: The core tasks—scheduling appointments, managing calendars and email, preparing documents, handling files, processing mail, and basic data entry—follow standardized patterns across organizations. While industry-specific variants (legal, medical, executive) require domain terminology knowledge, the underlying workflow logic and automation approach remains consistent; differences between employers are primarily configuration (which calendar system, which email client, which templates) rather than fundamental task redesign.

title: Tax examiners and collectors, and revenue agents
rationale: Tax examination and collection workflows follow standardized federal tax codes and procedures that are nearly identical across IRS, state, and local agencies, making the core audit and collection processes highly repeatable. The buyer market is heavily concentrated in government entities (46% federal, 34% state, 20% local), with the IRS representing the dominant purchaser, allowing a single vendor to serve most of the addressable value through shared infrastructure and configuration rather than complete rebuilds.
repeatability_rationale: Tax examination and collection work is fundamentally bound to each jurisdiction's proprietary tax systems, regulatory frameworks, and statutory requirements—federal, state, and local governments have distinct tax codes, enforcement procedures, and collection mechanisms that cannot be simply configured. An agent built for IRS federal income tax audits would require substantial rebuilding to handle state sales tax compliance or local property tax collection, as the underlying task logic, legal authorities, and system integrations differ materially across employers.

title: Travel agents
rationale: Travel agent workflows are highly standardized across companies—destination research, itinerary planning, booking via GDS systems, cost calculation, and visa/documentation guidance follow the same basic sequence everywhere. However, the buyer market is fragmented: value is spread across thousands of small independent agencies (11% self-employed), mid-sized regional travel firms, and corporate travel departments at diverse companies, with no dominant cohort large enough for a vendor to build a single configuration that captures most addressable spend.
repeatability_rationale: Travel agents perform core repeatable tasks across companies: gathering client preferences, searching availability systems, calculating costs, and making reservations across standardized platforms (GDS systems, hotel chains, airlines). While specific booking systems and agency processes vary, the underlying workflow—assess needs, search inventory, price, book, communicate confirmations—transfers readily with light configuration to different agencies or booking systems.
